title: Al-Muqaddimah al-Jazariyyah

sections.title: بَابُ النُّونِ وَالْمِيمِ الْمُشَدَّدَتَيْنِ وَالْمِيمِ السَّاكِنَةِ

bayt.english: The poet, Muhammad ibn al-Jazari al-Shafi'i, introduces himself as one hoping for his Lord's forgiveness.
He opens with praise of God and blessings upon His chosen Prophet.
He extends blessings to Muhammad, his family, his companions, and all who love and recite the Quran.
This poem is an introduction covering what every reciter of the Quran must know.
It is a strict duty on reciters to learn this knowledge before they begin reciting.
Namely the points where letters are articulated and their characteristics, so speech comes out most clearly.
It covers those skilled in tajweed and correct pausing, and what is drawn in the Uthmani script.

bayt.ajuz: وَتَاءِ أُنْثَى لَمْ تَكُنْ تُكْتَبْ بِـ: (هَا)
bayt.english: This includes every word written joined or separate, and the feminine ending written with ة rather than ه.
The articulation points of the Arabic letters number seventeen, according to the view chosen by those who studied it.
The open throat cavity produces alif and its two related long vowels, which trail off into open air.
From the deepest part of the throat come hamza and ha; from its middle come ain and ha.
From the throat's near end come ghayn and kha; qaf comes from the back of the tongue against the palate.
Kaf comes just below qaf; jim, shin, and ya from the tongue's middle; dad from the tongue's side edge.
Dad touches the molars on either the left or right side; lam runs along the tongue's edge to its tip.
Nun is placed just beneath the tongue's tip, and ra nearby but pressed further back.
Ta, dal, and another ta come from the tongue tip against the upper front teeth; the whistling letters sit nearby.
The whistling letters also touch the lower front teeth; za, dhal, and tha come from the upper front teeth's tips.
Those three come from the teeth's edges; fa comes from the inner lip meeting the upper front teeth.
Waw, ba, and meem come from the two lips together; the nasal ghunnah sound comes from the nasal passage.
Letters are described by pairs of opposite traits: voiced or voiceless, soft or hard, low or raised, open or closed, and more.
The voiceless letters are grouped in a memory phrase; the hardest, fully-stopped letters are grouped in another.

bayt.ajuz: وَسَبْعُ عُلْوٍ: خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ حَصَرْ
bayt.english: Between soft and hard sit the 'leen-like' letters in one phrase, and the seven 'raised' letters in another.
Sad, dad, ta, and za are the fully-pressed 'emphatic' letters; avoid weakening the fluent, easily-pronounced letters.
The whistling letters are sad, za, and sin; the letters with a little bounce are grouped in one phrase, plus the soft 'leen' letters.
Leen letters are a quiescent waw or ya preceded by a fatha.
Lam and ra have a deflected sound, ra also repeats slightly, shin spreads, and dad is drawn out lengthwise.
Applying tajweed properly is an absolute duty; whoever fails to recite the Quran correctly is at fault.
This is because God revealed the Quran this way, and it has reached us across generations in this same form.
Tajweed is also the ornament of recitation and the beauty of proper vocal performance.
Tajweed means giving every letter its full due, according to each of its characteristics and rights.
It means restoring each letter to its true origin, and pronouncing similar sounds consistently alike.
This should be done fully but naturally, with ease and gentleness, never forced or exaggerated.
The only thing separating correct recitation from incorrect is a person training and practicing their own mouth.
Distinguish the letters that stay low in the mouth, and avoid overly thickening the sound of alif.
Watch the hamza carefully in words like al-hamdu, a'udhu, ihdina, and Allah, and the lam in lillahi and lana.
Be gentle in phrases like wal-yatalattaf and ala Allah and wa la ad-dallin, and mind the meem in mahmasa and marad.
Mind the ba in barq, batal, bihim, and bidhi, keeping its firmness and full voicing.

bayt.sadr: فِيهَا وَفِي الْجِيمِ كَ: حُبِّ، الصَّبْرِ،
bayt.english: The same care applies to jim, as in hubb, al-sabr, ribwa, ijtuththat, hajj, and al-fajr.

bayt.ajuz: وَإِنْ يَكُنْ فِي الْوَقْفِ كَانَ أَبْيَنَا
bayt.english: Make the little bounce on quiescent letters clear, and even clearer when that letter falls at a stop.
Mind the ha in hashasa, uhittu, and al-haqq, and the sin in mustaqim, yastu, and yasqu.
Thin the sound of ra whenever it carries a kasra, and likewise when it is quiescent right after a kasra.

bayt.sadr: إِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ مِنْ قَبْلِ حَرْفِ اسْتِعْلَا،
bayt.english: This thinning applies unless a raised letter precedes it, or unless that kasra is not original to the word.
Scholars differ over the ra in the word 'firq'; also soften any doubled or repeated ra sound.

bayt.ajuz: عَنْ فَتْحٍ اوْ ضَمٍّ كَـ: عَبْدُ اللَّهِ
bayt.english: Thicken the lam in the word Allah when it follows a fatha or damma, as in 'Abdullah'.
Thicken every raised letter, especially when it is also fully pressed, as in the words qala and al-'asa.
Make the full pressing clear in words like ahattu and basatta; scholars differ on 'nakhluqkum'.
Take care to pronounce the quiescent letters clearly in ja'alna, an'amta, al-maghdub, and dalalna.
Keep the open, unpressed sound distinct in mahduran and 'asa, so they aren't confused with mahzuran and 'asa.
Preserve the full hardness of kaf and ta, as in shirkikum, tatawaffa, and fitana.

bayt.ajuz: أَدْغِمْ كَـ: قُل رَّبِّ، وَبَل لَّا، وَأَبِنْ:
bayt.english: When a letter meets an identical or similar quiescent letter, merge them, as in qur-rabbi and bal-la.

bayt.sadr: فِي يَوْمٍ، مَعْ قَالُوا وَهُم، وَقُل نَّعَمْ
bayt.english: Further merging examples are given, such as in yawmim ma'a, qalu wahum, qun-na'am, sabbihhu, and la tazigh qulub.
Distinguish dad from za by dad's drawn-out sound and its different point of articulation.

bayt.sadr: فِي: الظَّعْنِ، ظِلٍّ، الظُّهْرِ، عُظْمٍ، الْحِفْظِ،
bayt.english: Lists Quranic words containing za, such as al-za'n, zill, al-zuhr, and al-hifz, to help distinguish it from dad.
Continues listing more za words like zahir, laza, and zalama for practice distinguishing the two letters.

bayt.sadr: أَظْفَرَ، ظَنًّا كَيْفَ جَا، وَعَظَ سِوَى
bayt.english: Continues the za-word list, noting the word zalla is spelled with za in the surahs of Nahl and Zukhruf.
Notes further za spellings of zallta and zallu across different surahs, including one variant reading.
Lists more za words such as yazlalna and mahzuran, contrasted with the dad word fazzan.
Gives exceptions where a word looks like it should have za but is actually spelled with dad, like wayl and hal.
Notes al-hazz (with za) versus al-hadd (with dad) regarding food, and a known disagreement over the word danin.
Where a dad and a za letter meet in a phrase, pronouncing each one distinctly is required.
Lists a few more words, like udturra and saffin, needing careful distinct pronunciation of dad and za.
Pronounce the nasal ghunnah sound clearly whenever nun or meem is doubled, but hide the meem in one specific case.

bayt.ajuz: بَاءٍ عَلَى الْمُخْتَارِ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْأَدَا
bayt.english: Hide a quiescent meem with nasalization when it is followed by the letter ba, per the preferred method of reciters.

bayt.ajuz: وَاحْذَرْ لَدَى وَاوٍ وَفَا أَنْ تَخْتَفِي
bayt.english: Pronounce a quiescent meem clearly before every other letter, taking care it doesn't vanish before waw or fa.
A quiescent nun or tanwin follows one of four rulings: clear pronunciation, merging, conversion, or hiding.

bayt.ajuz: فِي اللَّامِ وَالرَّا لَا بِغُنَّةٍ لَزِمْ
bayt.english: Pronounce clearly before throat letters; merge without nasalization when followed by lam or ra.
Merge with nasalization before the letters of the word 'yu'minu', except within a single word like dunya.
Convert to a meem sound with nasalization before ba, and hide the sound before all remaining letters.
Lengthening of vowels comes in kinds: necessary, obligatory, and permissible, alongside plain shortening.

bayt.sadr: فَلَازِمٌ: إِنْ جَاءَ بَعْدَ حَرْفِ مَدّ
bayt.english: Necessary lengthening happens when a quiescent letter follows a long vowel, in both continuous and paused reading, held the longest.
Obligatory lengthening happens when a hamza follows the long vowel within the very same word.
Permissible lengthening happens when the hamza begins the next separate word, or when a pause creates a new quiescent ending.
After mastering correct pronunciation of the letters, one must also learn the proper places to pause.
Pausing and restarting fall into three kinds: complete, sufficient, and merely good.

bayt.sadr: وَهْيَ لِمَا تَمَّ، فَإِنْ لَمْ يُوجَدِ
bayt.english: A stop is complete where the meaning is finished; if meaning still depends on what follows, one should keep going.
Complete stops rank above sufficient ones; a good stop relies only on wording, mostly allowed at the end of verses.
Any stop that isn't complete, sufficient, or good is considered poor, only used when forced, and one restarts before it.

bayt.sadr: وَلَيْسَ فِي الْقُرْآنِ مِنْ وَقْفٍ يَجِبْ
bayt.ajuz: وَلَا حَرَامٌ غَيْرُ مَا لَهُ سَبَبْ
bayt.english: No pause in the Quran is truly mandatory or forbidden, except where there is a specific meaningful reason.

bayt.ajuz: فِي الْمُصْحَفِ الْإِمَامِ فِيمَا قَدْ أَتَى
bayt.english: One should also know which words are written joined or separate, and where the feminine ta appears, per the standard Mushaf.
Lists ten specific phrases that are written as two separate words despite sounding continuous, including 'an la' and 'la ilaha illa'.
Continues listing more phrases written separately across various surahs, including cases in Ya-Sin and the second mention in Hud.

bayt.sadr: أَنْ لَا يَقُولُوا، لَا أَقُولَ: إِنْ مَا:
bayt.english: Continues the list of separately-written phrases, then notes one case in Surat al-Ra'd that is written joined instead.

bayt.sadr: نُهُوا: أَقُطِعُوا: مِنْ مَا مَلَكَتْ: رُومَ النِّسَا
bayt.english: Lists further joined and separated spellings across several surahs, including a disputed case among reciters.

bayt.ajuz: وَأَن لَّمِ الْمَفْتُوحُ، كَسْرُ إِنَّ مَا:
bayt.english: Lists more separated and joined spellings, including a case with a kasra reading in Surat al-An'am.
Notes joined spellings in Surat al-An'am and disputed readings in Surahs al-Anfal and al-Nahl.

bayt.ajuz: رُدُّوا، كَذَا قُلْ بِئْسَمَا، وَالْوَصْلُ صِفْ
bayt.english: Lists a joined phrase with disputed spelling, plus other words confirmed as written joined.
Lists more words written joined, including cases across several different surahs.
Notes a specific joined spelling repeated in certain surahs, contrasted with words elsewhere written separately.
Notes that a word matching the pattern in Surat al-Nahl is written joined, with disputed readings in three other surahs.
Lists more words confirmed as written joined across several different surahs and contexts.

bayt.ajuz: عَن مَّن يَشَاءُ، مَن تَوَلَّى. يَوْمَ هُمْ
bayt.english: Continues listing joined words, then turns to words written as two separate words in specific contexts.
Lists more phrases written joined in the standard Mushaf, including demonstrative pronoun combinations.

bayt.ajuz: كَذَا مِنَ: أَلْ، وَيْ، وَهَلْ، لَا تَفْصِلِ
bayt.english: Confirms several more specific phrases and word-forms are written joined rather than separated.
Lists surahs where the word 'rahmat' is written with a regular ta rather than the rounded ة ending.
Continues listing more words across several surahs that take the regular ta ending instead of ة.
Continues the list of ta-ending exceptions across further named surahs, including the word for 'curse'.
Lists more ta-ending exceptions, including the word 'imra'at' (wife of) across several surahs.
Continues listing ta-ending exceptions, including 'shajarat' in Surat al-Dukhan and 'sunnat' in several surahs.
Lists further ta-ending exceptions including 'qurrat', 'jannat', 'fitrat', 'baqiyyat', 'ibnat', and 'kalimat'.
Notes one case in Surat al-A'raf, then states that any word disputed between singular and plural form takes the ta ending.

bayt.sadr: وَابْدَأْ بِهَمْزِ الْوَصْلِ مِنْ فِعْلٍ بِضَمّ؛
bayt.ajuz: إِنْ كَانَ ثَالِثٌ مِنَ الْفِعْلِ يُضَمّ
bayt.english: When starting a verb with a connecting hamza, pronounce it with damma if the verb's third root letter carries damma.
Pronounce that connecting hamza with kasra in other verb cases, and generally with kasra in nouns as well.
Lists nouns taking a kasra on the connecting hamza, such as ibn, ibnah, imru', ithnayn, imra'ah, ism, and ithnatayn.
Avoid stopping on a word while keeping its full final vowel sound, unless deliberately giving it a partial hint.
This applies except for fatha, where the vowel is dropped entirely, and a light hint is given for damma.
The poet declares his composition of this introduction complete, offered as a gift to every reciter of the Quran.
Its total verse count is one hundred and seven, and whoever masters tajweed will attain right guidance.
